title: "Data-driven archetypes of farmland change: Preliminary results"
author: Carolyn Koehn
abstract: |
  Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period. The processes leading to this conversion are variable and often highly localized. Uncertainty regarding the causal process of agricultural lands loss limits local efforts to address or mitigate the loss through agricultural lands protection. A better understanding of the different processes of agricultural lands loss and the associated factors can inform the development of effective, diverse toolboxes of agricultural lands protection to apply in different localities. In this chapter, I will use a multi-dimensional cluster analysis to identify archetypes of change over time in counties where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. I will draw on publicly-availabile data to calculate descriptive metrics for counties in southern Idaho's Snake River Plain. Identifying and understanding patterns and associated indicators of working lands loss will allow for more informed and effective working lands protection and development planning. Our workflow for identifying archetypes of agricultural land loss uses publicly available data and can be used in other threatened regions to describe and address processes of land use change.

# Context

Approximately 1.5 million km2 of land has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period (Radwan et al., 2021). The pathway to conversion is often attributed to urban or suburban sprawl (Chen et al., 2020; Eitel, 2003; van Vliet et al., 2017), and land use projections are based on the assumption that population growth will drive urban development of agricultural lands based on their proximity to an urban center (Xie et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2020; Haney and Cohen, 2015; Meiyappan et al., 2014). However, there are other pathways to agricultural land conversion, such as the expansion of rural settlements and industrial land, that are rarely addressed alongside urban sprawl in land use change literature (for exceptions, see Ju et al., 2018 and Jiang et al., 2019). While other pathways to agricultural land loss may not impact as large of a total area as urban sprawl, they have can have significant impacts, especially at local scales (Zhu et al., 2022).

The Snake River Plain of Idaho is a perfect place to study this phenomenon because it is experiencing different drivers of agricultural land conversion across its counties (though I am tempted to expand this to the West, as the same logic applies). We have observed pressures due to urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization. The purpose of this archetype analysis is to characterize the pathways to and outcomes of farmland loss as described by public data. These archetypes will aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring, contributing to better land use prediction models and a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities.

I’ve proposed to find these archetypes by using a cluster analysis. Cluster analyses are highly influenced by their data inputs, so it is necessary to justify the decisions to include every data indicator. I will use Ostrom’s social-ecological systems framework to identify a broad and relevant set of data indicators to include in the cluster analysis. I will also note possible data sources and available years, as I hope to create a clusters across both space and time (I hope to assign an archetype to each county about every 5 years to see if they change through time). I’ll be analyzing the resources units (broadly, the land), resource systems, and actors at the county level.

In this analysis, I create archetypes for 26 Idaho counties in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 (104 units total).

Archetypes of pathways to agricultural lands loss can aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring, contributing to better land use prediction models and a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities. The research questions from my proposal are:

1. Are there identifiable archetypes of agricultural lands loss in the western U.S.?
2. What are those archetypes, and which demographic, economic, and remotely sensed indicators are the most important characteristics of those archetypes?
3. Which of nature’s contributions to people are associated with and most threatened by different archetypes of land use change?

## Data Selection

In this analysis, I selected data that was available for these counties from 1990-2020. I linked data sources I knew to second-tier variables in Ostrom's social-ecological systems framework. For the full framework, including variables without data sources that I knew of and data sources I excluded because they do not inlude all analysis years, see the attached file `SES_data_outline.docx`.

```{r}
#| label: "load data"

# county data
aoi <- tigris::counties("ID", progress_bar = FALSE) %>%
  select(c("GEOID", "NAME")) %>%
  filter(NAME %in% c("Jefferson", "Gem", "Madison", "Clark", "Jerome", "Bonneville", "Teton", "Power", "Blaine", "Elmore", "Butte", "Adams", "Minidoka", "Bingham", "Ada", "Cassia", "Payette", "Fremont", "Bannock", "Twin Falls", "Owyhee", "Washington", "Gooding", "Lincoln", "Camas", "Canyon"))

# data retrieved from above sources
# see notebooks/data_retrieval.qmd for all methods
ru_data <- read.csv("data/RU_data.csv")
rs_data <- read.csv("data/RS_data.csv")
resource <- left_join(ru_data, rs_data) %>%
  filter(county %in% aoi$NAME)
actors <- read.csv("data/Actor_data.csv") %>%
  filter(county %in% aoi$NAME)

ses_data_list <- list(Resource = resource,
                      Actors = actors)
```

I scaled these data by mean normalization (divided by the range), so that all variables had a mean of 0 and range of [-1, 1]. In clustering, dividing by the range (scaling) is preferable to dividing by the standard deviation (normalization) to preserve possible cluster structure in the data [CITE].

```{r}
#| label: "scale data"

ses_data_list_sc <- lapply(ses_data_list, function(df) {
  df %>%
    na.omit() %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(across(!c(county, year),
                  ~ (.x - mean(.x)) / (max(.x) - min(.x))))
})
```


## Clustering

### Algorithmic Variable Selection

Before clustering begins, it is useful to select the most important variables for clustering. The `clustvarsel` package uses methods to select the most optimal subset of variables that contain cluster information and suggest variables that provide little extra information to drop. It's important to note that these are locally optimal -- depending on where in parameter space the algorithm randomly starts, it is possible that different variables may be selected. To account for this, I ran the variable selection algorithm 20 times and used the list of variables most frequently selected between the 20 runs.

I chose the most conservative method. The algorithm starts with all the variables, and tests dropping different variables from the equation to see if the difference is minimal.

I tested for a range of 1-9 possible clusters. 
<!-- It's recommended that the maximum number of clusters be set to the next highest integer from $n^{0.3}$ [CITE]. $104^{0.3} = 4.028$, so 5 is selected as the maximum. -->

```{r}
#| label: "variable selection bootstrap"
#| eval: false

ses_var_sel <- mapply(function(df, ses_system) {
  selected_vars <- data.frame(run = 1:20)
  selected_vars[,colnames(df)[-c(1:2)]] <- NA
  
  for (i in 1:20) {
    varsel <- clustvarsel(data = df[,-c(1:2)],
              G = 1:9,
              search = "greedy",
              direction = "backward",
              fit = FALSE)
    newrow <- (colnames(df)[-c(1:2)] %in% names(varsel$subset))
    selected_vars[i,2:ncol(selected_vars)] <- newrow
  }
  write.csv(selected_vars,
            paste0("data/bootstrap/", ses_system, "_var_sel.csv"),
            row.names = FALSE)
}, df = ses_data_list_sc, ses_system = names(ses_data_list_sc))
```

```{r}
#| label: "variable selection"

ses_data_sel <- mapply(function(df, ses_system) {
  selected_vars <- read.csv(paste0("data/bootstrap/", ses_system, "_var_sel.csv"))
  if(nrow(unique(selected_vars[,-1])) == 1) {
    varsel <- unique(selected_vars[,-1])
  } else { stop("Multiple variable selection possibilities") }
  
  df[,c(TRUE, TRUE, as.logical(varsel))]
}, df=ses_data_list_sc, ses_system = names(ses_data_list_sc),
SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
```

From the Resource clusters, the following variable was removed: percent developed land.

```{r}
#| include: false

print(colnames(ses_data_list_sc[["Resource"]])[!(colnames(ses_data_list_sc[["Resource"]]) %in% colnames(ses_data_sel[["Resource"]]))])
```

From the Actors clusters, the following variables were removed: the first and third principal components of the employment industries PCA (the second PC was retained), average age, percent of residents with a high school level education, and the farm tenure principal components.

```{r}
#| include: false

print(colnames(ses_data_list_sc[["Actors"]])[!(colnames(ses_data_list_sc[["Actors"]]) %in% colnames(ses_data_sel[["Actors"]]))])
```

### Gaussian Model-Based Clustering

To select a model, which includes selecting the number of groups and the shape, I used two different criteria (BIC and ICL) to test 14 different model shapes and 1-10 numbers of groups. We'd prefer to select $\leq5$ groups (next integer after $n^{0.3}$, CITE).

Since this clustering finds local maxima, it is sensitive to its initialization. I ran the cluster models 200 times for each SES subsystem, preserving the best model as the final result.

```{r}
#| label: "model selection"

ses_mclustBIC <- lapply(ses_data_sel, function(df) {
  BIC <- NULL
  LL <- NULL
  for(j in 1:200) {
    rBIC <- mclustBIC(df[,-c(1:2)], G=1:10, verbose=FALSE,
                    initalization = list(hcPairs=hcRandomPairs(df[,-c(1:2)])))
    rModel <- mclustModel(df[,-c(1:2)], BICvalues = rBIC)
    LL <- c(LL, rModel$loglik)
    BIC <- mclustBICupdate(BIC, rBIC)
  }
  list(mod=Mclust(df[,-c(1:2)], x = BIC), LL=LL)
})
```

<!-- for hist code, see https://centerstat.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/CAMM-mixture-modeling-demo-R-2021.pdf page 5-19 -->

`r ses_mclustBIC[["Resource"]]$mod$G` clusters is the best fit for the resource data. `r ses_mclustBIC[["Actors"]]$mod$G` clusters is the best fit for the resource data.

The log likelihood values from the bootstrapping process indicate that there are no competing models, so the final models are very likely to be the global as well as local maxima.

To get a sense for how the data are clustering, we can view their groups on a principal components graph.

```{r}
pca_viz <- lapply(ses_data_sel, function(df) {
  prcomp(df[,-c(1:2)])
})

factoextra::fviz_pca_biplot(
  pca_viz[["Resource"]],
  habillage=as.factor(ses_mclustBIC[["Resource"]]$mod$classification),
  title = "Resource",
  geom = "point", repel = TRUE,
  addEllipses = TRUE)
factoextra::fviz_pca_biplot(
  pca_viz[["Actors"]],
  habillage=as.factor(ses_mclustBIC[["Actors"]]$mod$classification),
  title = "Actors",
  geom = "point", repel = TRUE,
  addEllipses = TRUE)
```

# Preliminary Results

## Cluster Descriptions

### Resource Clusters

```{r}
#| label: "get CIs"
#| include: false

ci_clust <- mapply(function(mod, ses_system, input_data) {
  bootmod <- MclustBootstrap(mod$mod, nboot = 999, type = "bs")
  
  t(as.data.frame(summary(bootmod, "ci")$mean)) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    mutate(cluster = paste0(str_sub(ses_system, 1,1), str_sub(rownames(.), -1, -1)),
           input_data_name = str_sub(rownames(.), 1, -3))
}, mod = ses_mclustBIC, ses_system = names(ses_data_sel), input_data = ses_data_sel, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-R-CIs
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Characteristics of each Resource cluster. The means for each variable in each cluster are estimated by the 8-cluster model. 95% confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. Since variables were scaled, if the CI contains 0, the variable mean is not significantly different ($p>0.05$) than the overall mean across the study area (the Snake River Plain) and time period (1990-2020). Variables with significantly different means, suggesting that they are distinctive characteristics of that cluster, are shown in black."
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 6.5

# join with mean
as.data.frame(ses_mclustBIC[["Resource"]]$mod$parameters$mean) %>%
  mutate(input_data_name = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !input_data_name,
               names_to = "cluster",
               values_to = "mean") %>%
  mutate(cluster = str_replace(cluster, "V", substr("R",1,1))) %>%
  left_join(ci_clust[["Resource"]]) %>%
  mutate(sig = !(`2.5%`<0 & `97.5%`>0)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = input_data_name, colour = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, color = "grey70", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = `2.5%`, xmax = `97.5%`), show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(cluster)) +
  scale_color_manual(limits = c(TRUE, FALSE), values = c("black", "grey80")) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c("farm_size_pc2", "farm_size_pc1", "developed_change", "shrub_change", "forest_change", "cropland_change", "perc_farms_change", "housing_units_per_acre", "farms_per_acre", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "percent_shrubland", "percent_forest", "percent_cropland", "land_in_farms"),
                   labels = c("Farm Size (PC2)", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Developed Land Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Farms Loss/Gain", "Housing Density", "Farm Density", "Farms with Net Loss (%)", "Shrubland", "Forest", "Cropland", "Land in Farms")) +
  labs(x = "Mean", y = "Variable") +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
#| label: "label county data"

clust_dat <- mapply(function(df, mod, system_name) {
  left_join(df, aoi[,c("NAME", "geometry")], by = c("county" = "NAME")) %>%
    st_as_sf() %>%
    cbind(., mod$mod$classification) %>%
    mutate(cluster = paste0(substr(system_name,1,1), mod.mod.classification)) %>%
    select(-mod.mod.classification)
}, df = ses_data_list, mod = ses_mclustBIC, system_name=names(ses_data_list))
```

\newpage
#### Cluster R1: Growing urban center and suburbs push out large farms

```{r}
r1 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R1")

r1_means <- r1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R1, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Lower than average cropland cover (13.9%) and land in farms (26.4%)
- Lower than average shrubland and forest cover (17.4% and 0.351%, respectively)
- More farms with net losses (71.3%)
- Higher than average farm units per acre (0.00184 farms per acre)
- A higher than average density of housing units (0.206 units per acre)
- Higher developed area gain (+1.12% in previous 5-year period) and cropland loss (-1.07%)
- Slightly lower forest gain than average (+0.000922%)
- A lower value of farm size principal component 1 translates to a higher amount of smaller farms (1-50 acres)

Cluster R1 only consists of Ada County, in all years of this analysis (1990-2020). In R1, urban and suburban growth compete with large farms. Small farms can cater to the urban population (see cluster A?) through farmer's markets, but larger farms are pushed out. Developed land increases (Ada county grows from 10% to 18% developed land from 1990 to 2020), while cropland decreases equivalently (18% to 10%). Forests and shrublands are not lost, and in fact have very small gains, because of demand for recreation. 

```{r}
clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990)) %>%
  mutate(year = "1990-2020") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("thistle3", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster R2: Agriculture persists where it's possible

```{r}
r2 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R2")

r2_means <- r2 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R2, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Lower than average cropland cover (7.37%) and land in farms (22.6%)
- Higher forest cover on average (19.6%). Some counties in R2 have as low as 0% forest and others are as high as 52%, so this is not a uniting characteristic.
- Lower than average housing and farm density (0.00361 and 0.000261 units per acre, respectively)
- Lower than average cropland loss (-0.157%) and lower developed land gain (+0.0565%)
- A higher value of farm size principal component 1 translates to higher amounts of medium to large farms (180-2000+ acres)

Cluster R2 consists of Adams, Blaine, Camas, Clark, Elmore, Fremont, Lincoln, and Washington counties across all the study years (1990-2020), In 2010, Owyhee county joins this group. Agriculture is well established where it can be (larger farms, yet low cropland cover and land in farms) and wild or grazing lands (forest and shrubland) persist where cropland conversion would be unprofitable. These counties also include small developed areas that are growing slowly.

```{r}
clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2010)) %>%
  mutate(year = ifelse(year==1990, "1990-2000", "2010-2020")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "thistle3", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

#### Cluster R3: Agricultural area accomodating increasing residential use

```{r}
r3 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R3")

r3_means <- r3 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R3, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average land in farms (75.6%) and cropland (67.2%)
- Lower than average forest and shrubland (0.0117% and 1.78%, respectively)
- High amount of farms with net loss (67%)
- Higher housing and farm density (0.176 and 0.00609 units per acre, respectively)
- Higher gain of farms (+0.0856% increase in farms)
- Higher cropland loss (-1.8%)
- Higher than average developed land gain (+1.63%)
- Minimally lower than average forest loss (-0.00131%), minimally higher than average shrubland gain (+0.193%)
- Lower scores for both farm size PCs 1 and 2 translates to a higher amount of very small farms (1-10 acres)

Cluster R3 consists of only Canyon County in 2000-2020. Canyon County has a large agricultural economy, with lots of cropland and land in farms, many small farms, and less wild lands. In recent years, it has been losing cropland and gaining developed land, with its higher housing density indicating that it is a desirable place to live as well as farm.

```{r}

  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "white", "thistle3", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +

```

#### Cluster R4: Agriculture declines in a mixed landscape

```{r}
r4 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R4")

r4_means <- r4 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R4, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average land in farms (52.%) and cropland (29.7%)
- Higher than average forestland (19.6%); Canyon County in 1990 at <1% is the exception
- Higher farm density (0.00146 farms per acre)
- Higher cropland loss (-1.11%)
- A lower value of farm size principal component 1 translates to a higher amount of smaller farms (1-50 acres)

Cluster R4 consists of Bannock, Bonneville, Gem, Madison, and Teton counties for 1990-2020, as well as Canyon County in 1990. R4 has both high agriculture and forest use, but cropland declines while all other land covers (forest, shrub, developed) increase. In this mixed use landscape, only agriculture (many of which are small farms) seems to decline.

```{r}
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
```

#### Cluster R5: Little change in rural agriculture and shrublands

```{r}
r5 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R5")

r5_means <- r5 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R5, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average land in farms (54.6%) and cropland (24.5%)
- Lower than average forestland (4.65%) but higher than average shrubland (48.8%)
- Lower than average housing and farm density (0.00643 and 0.000554 units per acre, respectively)
- Lower than average developed land gain (+0.0905%)
- A lower value of farm size principal component 2 indicates a tendency toward very small or very large farms, but few medium farms.

Cluster R5 consists of Bingham, Cassia, and Power counties for 1990-2020. Between low housing and farm density and high farmland and shrubland, these counties are a rural mixture of agriculture and shrublands. Almost all land use changes are near the study area average (shrubland: -0.2%, forestland: 0.04%, cropland: -1.16%). Developed land is growing more slowly than average.

```{r}
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R6, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Much lower than average land in farms (10.4%) and cropland (4.52%)
- Low forestland (6.43%) and high shrubland (76%)
- Low farms with net losses (39.4%)
- Lower than average housing and farm density (0.000870 and 0.000125 units per acre, respectively)
- Lower than average cropland loss (-0.0826%) and developed land gain (+0.0256%)
- A higher value for farm size PCs 1 and 2 translates to a tendency towards medium sized farms (50-500 acres)

Cluster R6 consists of Butte County, and Owyhee County in 1990-2000. This cluster is similar to R2, with lower farmland, forestland, and developed land, and higher shrubland. Here, however, medium size farms are more common, and they're more likely to make a profit.

```{r}
clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2020)) %>%
  mutate(year = ifelse(year==2000, "1990-2000", "2010-2020")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "thistle3", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster R7: Stable mix of crops, shrublands, and development

```{r}
r7 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R7")

r7_means <- r7 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R7, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average cropland (30.9%). Land in farms is about average (40.5%). IN this cluster, most land in farms is used for cropland.
- Lower than average forestland (0.268%), higher than average shrubland (46.5%)
- Lower than average housing density (0.0169 housing units per acre)
- Lower than average cropland loss (-0.207%)
- Lower than average forest gain (+0.012%)
- Lower than average developed land gain (+0.176%)

Cluster R7 consists of Jefferson and Twin Falls counties for 1990-2020. They have lots of croplands and shrublands, as well as some developed lands like the city of Twin Falls (on average, developed lands cover 4.05% of these counties). Unlike other clusters, all land covers in this group are quite stable, with very little change preceding each analyzed year.

```{r}
clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2000)) %>%
  mutate(year = "1990-2020") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "thistle3", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster R8: Concentration of agriculture

```{r}
r8 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R8")

r8_means <- r8 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Resource cluster R8, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average land in farms (52%) and cropland (37.1%)
- Lower than average forestland (0.00278%) and shrubland (18.1%)
- Higher than average farm density (0.00164 farms per acre) but lower than average housing density (0.0196 housing units per acre)
- Lower than average loss of farms (8.87% decline)
- Lower than average cropland loss (-0.174%), and lower than average forest gain (0.00278%)
- A lower value of farm size principal component 1 translates to a higher amount of smaller farms (1-50 acres)

Cluster R8 consists of Gooding, Jerome, Minidoka, and Payette counties for 1990-2020. There is a concetration of agriculture here, with higher land in farms, cropland, and farm density, and lower housing density and forest and shrubland cover. While on average every county is losing farms, these counties are losing farms at a slower rate.

### Actors Clusters

Although this analysis identifies 8 resource archetypes in the study area, it only identified 4 actors archetypes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-A-CIs
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Characteristics of each Actors cluster. The means for each variable in each cluster are estimated by the 4-cluster model. 95% confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. Since variables were scaled, if the CI contains 0, the variable mean is not significantly different (p>0.05) than the overall mean across the study area (the Snake River Plain) and time period (1990-2020). Variables with significantly different means, suggesting that they are distinctive characteristics of that cluster, are shown in black."
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 6.5

# join with mean
as.data.frame(ses_mclustBIC[["Actors"]]$mod$parameters$mean) %>%
  mutate(input_data_name = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !input_data_name,
               names_to = "cluster",
               values_to = "mean") %>%
  mutate(cluster = str_replace(cluster, "V", substr("A",1,1))) %>%
  left_join(ci_clust[["Actors"]]) %>%
  mutate(sig = !(`2.5%`<0 & `97.5%`>0)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = input_data_name, colour = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, color = "grey70", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = `2.5%`, xmax = `97.5%`), show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(cluster)) +
  scale_color_manual(limits = c(TRUE, FALSE), values = c("black", "grey80")) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c("pop_urban", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "Bachelors", "unemployment_rate", "emply_pc2", "perc_pop_change", "pop_per_acre"),
                   labels = c("Urban Population (%)", "Farms with Net Loss (%)", "Residents with Bachelors", "Unemployment Rate", "Industry Employment (PC2)", "Population Loss/Gain", "Population Density")) +
  labs(x = "Mean", y = "Variable") +
  theme_classic()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster A1: More urbanites

```{r}
a1 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A1")

a1_means <- a1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A1, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average population density (0.194 persons per acre) and higher population gain (+28.4%)
- Higher than average percentage of residents with at least a Bachelors degree (29.5%)
- Higher than average amount of farms with a net loss (59.7%)
- Higher than average percentage of the population living in an urban area (58.3%)
- The average PCA results indicate that in A1 many people are employed in services. construction and finance/insurance/real estate are also more likely. People tend not to be employed in manufacturing and wholesale trade.

Cluster A1 consists of Ada, Blaine, and Canyon counties in 1990-2020, Bannock and Bonneville counties in 1990-2010, Teton and Madison counties in 2000-2020, and Elmore County in 2000. In these counties and years, the number of actors in the system is increasing quickly. Most of the population is living in urban areas, and many have graduated college. The farming actors are at a financial disadvantage, as on average 60% of their farms are operating at a net loss.

```{r}
clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  # filter(year %in% c(2000)) %>%
  # mutate(year = "1990-2020") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkseagreen3", "white", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster A2: Manufacturing provides additional rural employment

```{r}
a2 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A2")

a2_means <- a2 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A2, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- A higher value of industry employment PC2 translates to a high percentage of people employed in manufacturing, and to a lesser degree, in services and in transportation and public utilities.
- Lower unemployment rate (4.91%)
- Higher percentage of people with a Bachelors degree (24.6%)
- More farms with net losses (64.2%)
- Lower urban population (13.9%)

Cluster A2 consists of 8 counties in 2020: Bannock, Bingham, Bonneville, Elmore, Gem, Jefferson, Payette, and Twin Falls. Many here are employed in manufacturing, or support manufacturing in the services and transportation sectors. With many farms operating at a net loss, manufacturing can offer off-farm employment. A majority of the actors in these counties are living in rural areas, few are unemployed, and many have college degrees.

```{r}
clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2020)) %>%
  # mutate(year = "1990-2020") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "darkseagreen3", "white", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster A3: Slow growing population in urban areas

```{r}
a3 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A3")

a3_means <- a3 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A3, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Lower population density (0.0286 persons per acre) and lower population growth (+8.15%)
- Less residents have a Bachelors degree (14.1%)
- Less farms operate at a net loss (47.8%)
- Higher percent of population living in urban areas (42.1%)
- A higher value of industry employment PC2 translates to a high percentage of people employed in manufacturing, and to a lesser degree, in services and in transportation and public utilities. This value is not as high as in A2, so manufacturing is not as large of an industry. Here, PC1 is lower than in A2, indicating that the services industry in A3 employs less people. The mean PC values for PCs 1 and 2 also indicate that A3 employs a slightly higher percentage of people in agriculture.

Cluster A3 consists of Cassia, Fremont, Gooding, Jerome, Minidoka, Power, and Washington counties for 1990-2020. For 1990-2010, but not 2020, Bingham, Gem, Jefferson, Payette, and Twin Falls counties are in this cluster (these all transition to A2 in 2020). Owyhee County is in A3 for 2000-2020. A few counties also briefly are in A3: Clark and Lincoln counties in 2020, Madison and Teton counties in 1990, and Elmore County in 1990 and 2010 (Elmore also transitions to A2 in 2020).

The defining characteristic of this archetype seems to be slow population growth and low population density where more of the population lives in urban areas (compared to A4, where population growth is also slow but the population is more rural). 

```{r}
clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  # filter(year %in% c(2020)) %>%
  # mutate(year = "1990-2020") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "white", "darkseagreen3", "white")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  theme_void()
```

\newpage
#### Cluster A4: Slow growing population in rural areas

```{r}
a4 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A4")

a4_means <- a4 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),

               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A4, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Low population density (0.0027 persons per acre) and low population growth (+5.93%)
- Lower percentage of residents with Bachelors degree (15.6%)
- Very low urban population (0.745%)
- A low value for employment industries PC2 indicates low employment in manufacturing, services, and wholesale trade. The averaged PCA results for A4 suggest higher employment in agriculture and construction.

Cluster A4 consists of Adams, Butte, and Camas counties in 1990-2020, as well as Clark and Lincoln counties in 1990-2010, and Owyhee County in 1990. The low population density and low urban population suggest that this archetype is very rural, and the population here grows more slowly.

```{r}

  theme_void()
```
